title: The Morning Snow Report
text:
Good morning, everyone! This is Weather Wendy with your snow report. Last night, our town got {number} inches of fresh snow. The snow is very {adjective} today, which is perfect for snowmen and sled rides.

Right now it is cold outside, so please wear your coat, your hat, and two pairs of {plural noun}. The wind is blowing {adverb} from the north, and it smells a little bit like {food}.

Later this afternoon, we expect clouds shaped like {plural noun} and a small chance of snowflakes the size of a {noun}. Kids may want to {verb} in the front yard before lunch.

Tonight, the moon will be big and {adjective}. Make sure to drink something warm and say goodnight to your snowman. This has been Weather Wendy. Stay warm and keep {verb ending in ing}!

title: A Message from Principal Plum
text:
Good morning, families. This is Principal Plum. Because of all the snow, school is closed today. The parking lot is covered in snow up to my {body part}, and the buses are stuck behind a giant pile of {plural noun}.

I know many of you are sad to miss school. Do not worry about our class gerbil, Peanut. Mr. Diaz went in early to feed him and give him a tiny {adjective} blanket. Peanut {past tense verb} to say thank you.

Please use this day to read a book, drink warm cocoa, and {verb} with your family. If you build a snowman, you may bring a picture to class. The most {adjective} snowman will win a {noun} for the whole class.

Stay safe, stay warm, and please wear your {color} mittens. Tomorrow, please walk into school {adverb} and stomp the snow off your {plural noun}.

title: How to Build the Best Snowman
text:
Building a snowman is easy if you follow these steps. Ask a grown-up to help you with the heavy parts.

First, roll a big ball of snow for the bottom. Keep rolling until it is as big as a {noun}. Then make a medium ball for the middle and a small one for the head. Stack them up {adverb} so they do not fall over.

Next, give your snowman a face. Use two {plural noun} for the eyes and a carrot for the nose. For the mouth, make a smile out of little {plural noun}. If you do not have any, you can use {food} instead.

Last, dress him up. Wrap a {color} scarf around his neck and put an old {noun} on his head. Give him two sticks for arms so he can {verb} at the cars going by. Now step back and look at him. He is so {adjective}! If you listen closely, you might even hear him {verb ending in ing}.

title: Grandpa's Snow Day Cocoa
text:
On every snow day, Grandpa makes his famous hot cocoa. Here is his recipe, written down by me.

First, Grandpa pours two cups of milk into a pot. He says you must stir it {adverb} or the milk gets {adjective}. Then he adds three big spoonfuls of cocoa powder and one tiny pinch of {plural noun}. That is his secret.

While it warms up, Grandpa likes to {verb} around the kitchen and hum a song about {plural noun}. He says it makes the cocoa taste better. I think he just likes {verb ending in ing}.

When the cocoa is warm, pour it into your favorite mug. Put marshmallows on top, plus a {noun} if you are feeling fancy. Drink it slowly while you look out the window at the {adjective} snow. Grandpa always closes his eyes after his first sip and says, "{exclamation}! That is {adjective}!"

title: My Snow Day Diary
text:
Dear Diary,
When I woke up this morning, everything outside was white! Mom looked out the window and said school was closed. I was so happy that I {past tense verb} all the way down the stairs.

After breakfast, my brother and I put on our snow pants, boots, and {plural noun}. It took us {number} minutes. By the time we got outside, I was already a little bit {adjective}.

First we made snow angels in the front yard. Mine looked like a {adjective} {animal}. Then we had a contest with our neighbor, Mrs. Kim, to see who could throw a snowball the highest. She is very {adjective} at throwing. Our dog, Muffin, jumped into a snow pile and came out looking like a {noun}.

Now I am inside, drinking cocoa and watching the snow fall {adverb}. My cheeks are pink, and my toes feel like {plural noun}. I hope tomorrow is a snow day too, so I can {verb} all over again.

title: The Great Sled Race Results
text:
Here are the official results of the Great Sled Race on Maple Hill. The judges were Mr. Lopez and his cat, who watched from the window.

In third place is Sam. Sam rode a red plastic sled and shouted "{exclamation}!" the whole way down. He wins a cup of cocoa and a {adjective} sticker.

In second place is Priya. She rode down the hill on a {noun} and finished in {number} seconds. The judges say she was very {adjective}. She wins a pair of fuzzy {plural noun}.

In first place is Grandma Bea! She rode the wooden sled she had when she was little and went down {adverb}. At the bottom, she {past tense verb} and waved to the crowd. She wins the golden trophy and a big bag of {plural noun}. Next year, everyone wants to {verb} like Grandma Bea.

title: Rules for Our Snow Fort
text:
My friends and I built a snow fort in my backyard. It has two rooms, a window, and a flag made from a {color} sock. To keep it safe and fun, we made some rules.

Rule one: Everyone must say the secret word before coming in. This week, the secret word is "{silly word}." Rule two: No more than {number} kids inside at once, or the walls start to wiggle.

Rule three: Please do not {verb} inside the fort. Last time, Theo did that and the roof dripped on his {noun}. Rule four: Snacks are allowed, but only crackers and {plural noun}. Crumbs make the floor {adjective}.

Rule five: When it is time to go inside, we all say goodbye to the fort {adverb}. Then we drink cocoa and dream about {verb ending in ing} in the snow tomorrow. Our fort is the most {adjective} place in the whole neighborhood!

title: Dear Snow, Please Come Back
text:
Dear Snow,
Thank you for coming to our town last week. You were very {adjective}, and you covered everything, even our mailbox and Dad's {noun}. We had the best time.

My sister and I made a snowman named Mr. Pebble. He had two {plural noun} for eyes and a big {adjective} smile. We also made {number} snow angels in a row. Mom took a picture and hung it on the fridge.

Now you have melted, and the yard is just mud and {plural noun}. Mr. Pebble's scarf is still lying in the grass. I {past tense verb} a little when I saw it.

Please come back soon. If you do, I promise to {verb} with you all day and wear my mittens the whole time. I will even leave a bowl of {food} on the porch for you. Please write back {adverb}.
Love,
Owen

title: How to Get Ready for the Snow
text:
Going out in the snow takes a lot of work. My mom made this list so I do not forget anything.

First, put on your warmest shirt and your thick socks. Then pull on your snow pants. You may need to {verb} to get them all the way up. They are puffy and make a {adjective} sound when you walk. Next, put on your coat and zip it all the way up to your {body part}.

Now it is time for boots. Push your feet in {adverb}. If they will not go in, check for {plural noun} hiding inside. Last time, I found one of my brother's {plural noun} in there. After that, put on your hat, your scarf, and your mittens. By now you will look like a big {adjective} {noun}.

Last of all, open the door and step outside. Take two steps in the snow and start {verb ending in ing}. Then Mom will knock on the window and say it is time to come in for {food}.

title: A Snowman Tells All
text:
Today our school newspaper talked to Frosty Fred, the snowman who stands in front of the library. Here is what he said.

We asked Fred how he feels about snow days. "I love them," he said. "Kids come out and give me {plural noun} and a new {noun} to wear. Yesterday, a girl named Kaya gave me a hug so {adjective} that I almost lost my nose."

We asked Fred what he does at night. "Mostly I stand here," he said. "Sometimes I watch the {plural noun} go by. When nobody is looking, I like to {verb} a little. Last night, I {past tense verb} until the sun came up."

Finally, we asked Fred if he has any advice for kids. "Always wear your mittens," he said {adverb}. "Eat a warm bowl of {food} after playing outside. And please, never let the {animal} near my carrot nose." Thank you, Fred. Stay {adjective}!
